title: Solubility Rules Quiz
disclaimer: This quiz uses a selected intro-chemistry solubility table. It is for practice, not a complete or universal set of rules. Textbooks disagree on some cases (for example Ca(OH)₂, Sr(OH)₂, Ag₂SO₄, and MgS). Always follow your instructor’s table when they differ. Ions typically required from memory are left off the table.

referenceTable.title: Selected Solubility Information
referenceTable.note: Excludes ions typically required from memory: Group 1 cations, NH₄⁺, NO₃⁻, and acetate are soluble.

cells: Ag⁺, Pb²⁺, Hg₂²⁺, Ca²⁺, Sr²⁺, Ba²⁺

questions.explanation: Chlorides are soluble in most cases. Na⁺ is also a Group 1 cation, one of the always-soluble ions typically required from memory.
Most chlorides are soluble, but Ag⁺ is a listed exception. AgCl is a classic insoluble chloride.
Chlorides are generally soluble except with Ag⁺, Pb²⁺, and Hg₂²⁺. PbCl₂ is one of those insoluble exceptions.
The chloride exceptions are Ag⁺, Pb²⁺, and mercury(I), Hg₂²⁺. Hg₂Cl₂ is insoluble; do not confuse Hg₂²⁺ with Hg²⁺.
Most bromides and iodides are soluble. K⁺ is also a Group 1 cation, so KI is soluble on both counts.
Bromides and iodides are insoluble with Ag⁺, Pb²⁺, Hg²⁺, and Hg₂²⁺. AgI is a standard insoluble iodide.
Pb²⁺ is an exception for both chlorides and iodides. PbI₂ is insoluble.
Unlike chlorides, bromides and iodides also list Hg²⁺ as insoluble. HgI₂ is insoluble on this table.
Most sulfates are soluble. Cu²⁺ is not among the sulfate exceptions (Ag⁺, Pb²⁺, Hg₂²⁺, Ca²⁺, Sr²⁺, Ba²⁺).
Sulfates of Ba²⁺, Sr²⁺, and Ca²⁺ are insoluble on this table. BaSO₄ is the usual example.
Ca²⁺ is a listed insoluble sulfate cation. This course table treats CaSO₄ as insoluble.
This course table includes Ag⁺ among the insoluble sulfate cations. Some other books call Ag₂SO₄ only slightly soluble.
Carbonates are insoluble in most cases. The few soluble ones are the always-soluble cations such as Group 1 Na⁺.
Ammonium is treated as always soluble. Even though most carbonates are insoluble, (NH₄)₂CO₃ is one of the few that dissolve.
Most carbonates are insoluble. Ca²⁺ is not an always-soluble cation, so CaCO₃ is insoluble.
Phosphates follow the same pattern as carbonates: most are insoluble. Ca₃(PO₄)₂ is insoluble.
This course table lists Ba²⁺ as the soluble hydroxide (besides always-soluble cations). Ba(OH)₂ is soluble here.
Only Ba²⁺ is listed as a soluble hydroxide on this table. Ca(OH)₂ is therefore insoluble here, even though some textbooks call it slightly soluble.
Most hydroxides are insoluble. Fe³⁺ is not Ba²⁺ or an always-soluble cation, so Fe(OH)₃ is insoluble.
This course table treats Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, Sr²⁺, and Ba²⁺ sulfides as soluble. MgS is soluble here; some other books list it as insoluble.
Alkaline-earth sulfides are the soluble exceptions on this table. BaS is soluble.
Most sulfides are insoluble. Cu²⁺ is not among Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, Sr²⁺, or Ba²⁺, so CuS is insoluble.
Nitrate salts are treated as soluble. Nitrate is one of the ions typically required from memory and left off the exception table.
